This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which found no division-specific legal, incident or enforcement signal: its 2024 share of national LGBTIQ+ discrimination cases was 0.84% (an advocacy group's regional table). Its recorded case trend follows the national one, which rose in 2025 to a record; a low share is not evidence of safety — most regions outside the two biggest rose that year.

There is no division-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding for this division; its recorded profile comes from the shared national case table. National frame: 2025 produced a record 3,620 discrimination cases on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression (+27.1%; 23% of all cases in 24 years), and 2024 was the first regression since the return of democracy. Protective national framework (a gender-identity law in force 2019, same-sex marriage 2022, an anti-discrimination law) sits against concrete 2025-26 rollback (a gender-identity support programme excluded from the 2026 budget; a health-ministry circular restricting that programme for minors; a legislative initiative against trans children's rights) and administrative document friction from civil-registry identification-system issuance failures (an official audit, 2025), which is directly relevant to a traveller whose documents must match presentation.

An advocacy group's annual report (2025 edition, published March 2026) supplies this record's division-specific figures from its national regional table: this division is placed at 1.04% of nationally documented abuse cases, with a +14.28% year-on-year rise in 2025. Nationally, the report records a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025 (+27.1%, the highest in 24 years), with only two regions falling while the other 14 rose; it reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which is what this record's mid-share reading rests on. The 2024 share cited in this record's comparison is not reproduced in this 2025 edition.

It independently confirms the record's national-frame claims (a gender-identity law in force 2019, marriage since 2022, anti-discrimination law) with dates and a document-change mechanism directly relevant to a traveller whose identity papers must match their presentation.

rewrites.blindSummary:
On 19 April 2025 a 48-year-old trans woman was found dead in a room of a hostel in this department; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in this department in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.
rewrites.blindTangential: A national law enacted in 2025 restricts entry to public bathrooms according to sexual orientation; being national legislation it applies in this department too and is a direct visitor-facing hazard for gender-nonconforming travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (27 May 2025): a 48-year-old trans woman was found dead in a hostel room in this department on 19 April 2025, the autopsy recording death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways, after entering the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and left about two hours later; the case is being investigated as a possible hate crime — an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. Her family and local LGBTIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Context offered: this country has no gender-identity-recognition legislation and no law sanctioning hate crimes, and activists note a recently promulgated legislative proposal restricting access to public bathrooms by sexual orientation; the public prosecutor's office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021 (most victims gay men 55.8%, trans women 36.4%).

A news outlet (updated 21 May 2025): a 48-year-old trans woman was found dead inside a hostel in this department after entering on a Sunday with a man who later left alone carrying a white bag; she was initially processed as NN until identified through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route; relatives denounced the crime and demanded police action. The body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired; no suspect had been identified in the audited text.

rewrites.blindSummary: This frontier department is covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding beyond the national and departmental homicide counts: no deviation from the national position is material enough to score separately, so it is assessed at the national score. Context that does apply here: this department sits in the country's frontier/border belt where 'public-order' regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct, and an advocacy group's 2025 report documents the expansion of violence and insufficiency of government response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others.
rewrites.blindTangential: Armed-group 'social cleansing' campaigns name gays, lesbians and trans women alike (a flyer pattern, 2024), so LGB-wide hostility from non-government armed actors shapes the same risk environment; trans women are the named priority targets, but the campaign is not trans-exclusive.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: Displacement of trans women from frontier departments by armed groups is resident-impact — losing home and livelihood; a visitor's exposure is different in kind: transit and intercity roads through zones controlled by armed groups rather than losing a residence.
blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (6 Aug 2025) follow-up in a reporting series: a viral video shocked the country but the killings continued — armed gangs; frames being queer in parts of the country as 'to sign your own death sentence'. National context.

A news outlet (30 Jul 2024) documented armed groups in a department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via a messaging app named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. It reports eight trans women were killed in this country between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. No department-specific finding appears; the violence-and-displacement pattern by armed actors is the claim this record relies on.

An encyclopedia's national-framework article governing what a visitor stands under in this department, whose own dossier records no department-specific trans finding. It records that consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the national legislature passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011; the right to change legal gender has existed since 1993, and since 2015 gender change is possible without psychiatric or physical evaluations. The constitutional court legalized same-sex marriage in April 2016 and granted same-sex couples full adoption rights in 2015; transgender people have been allowed to serve openly in the military since 2015. It also reports this country's society as 'generally conservative' on LGBT issues, with an October 2019 poll reaching 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time (47% opposed). The article carries no department-specific fact, so like the record's existing news sources it grounds the national framework a visitor in this frontier department stands under rather than a department-level finding.
